title: You are right too
hook: as judge he tells both quarreling men they're right, and when his wife objects, tells her she's right too (Nasruddin tale)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nasruddin rode his donkey backward so he could see his students. Your line was face the other way. Did you turn around once and look at the road behind you? Day thirty-nine.

Two friends, a couple, two coworkers, a family group chat. An argument breaks out, and both sides turn to whoever is watching: tell them I'm right. Pick a side. Be the judge. Somebody has to win. In the old stories, Nasruddin gets this job for real. For a while, the tales say, he serves as the town's judge, the qadi. Two men walk into his courtroom, red in the face, each sure the other has wronged him. Nasruddin settles into his seat and listens. And what he says next is the whole joke. Today's story is you are right too.
screen: `TELL THEM I'M RIGHT.` → `NASRUDDIN, THE JUDGE.` → `TWO MEN, RED IN THE FACE.`

segments.voice: The first man tells his side. It's convincing. Nasruddin nods and says: you're right. The second man jumps in, furious, and tells his side. It's convincing too. Nasruddin nods and says: you're right. Then his wife, who has been listening from the next room, and in some tellings it's a clerk or a neighbor, can't stand it. They can't both be right! And Nasruddin turns to her, thinks it over, and says: you know, you're right too. That's the whole story, and it's a joke first. Let it be a joke. But look at what it catches. We tend to hear an argument as a contest with one winner, and we pick our winner fast, often before the second person has finished talking. Nasruddin can't do it. Each time someone speaks, he actually hears them, and each time he finds something true. Quarrels are often like that. Each side is holding a real piece: a real hurt, a real fact, a real fear. The story also cuts the other way, and it's worth saying so. A judge who agrees with everyone has decided nothing. The men still have their quarrel. Some things do need a decision, and the tale is laughing at Nasruddin too. So it isn't telling you never to choose. It's asking you to notice how fast you choose, and what you miss when you do. Listen long enough to say, honestly, you're right, about something, to each person. Then decide, if you have to.
screen: `YOU'RE RIGHT. AND YOU'RE RIGHT.` · `WE PICK A WINNER FAST.` · `EACH SIDE HOLDS A REAL PIECE.` · `A JUDGE WHO DECIDES NOTHING.` · then, large: `YOU'RE RIGHT TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hear two sides without deciding. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a disagreement you're close to, yours or someone else's. Let the first person speak, in your head, and find one thing they're right about. Just one. Then let the other person speak, and find one thing they're right about. If you're one of the two, find the thing the other person is right about. Don't decide who wins. Hold both, the way Nasruddin does, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
You are right too. Nasruddin the judge, finding something true in each person who speaks, even the one who says they can't both be right. Today's word.
Your line: you are also right. Today, in one disagreement, before you answer, say out loud what the other person is right about. Then carry on. Day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: Nasruddin's judge stories are told across Turkey, Iran and Central Asia, often to children and in classrooms, as a joke about snap judgments; in some tellings the objector is his wife, in others a clerk or a neighbor.

original.note: Arabic, qadi: a judge. In Turkish it became kadı, the title Nasruddin holds in these tales.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly judge who can't make up his mind.
what it means: most quarrels have a real piece on each side, and we pick a winner before we've heard them.
what a scholar hears: the qadi, the town judge, is a stock role in Nasruddin tales, and the joke works on both the listener and the judge.
